strings.title: Make the Next Ten
strings.label: Day 1
strings.strategy: Add up to the next ten first, then add what is left.
strings.keywords: next ten, friendly number, break apart, jump
strings.connection: First string of the week. Sets up the open number line and the idea that 10 ones make a ten.
watchFor: Counting on by ones (28, 29, 30, 31...): accept it, then ask "Is there a jump that gets you to a ten?"
Breaking the number the wrong way (28 + 5 as 28 + 3 + 2 = 33, but stopping at 31): ask "How much of the 5 have you used?"
Not knowing the partners of 10: keep a quick reference (8 and 2, 7 and 3...) and celebrate students who use them.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did the first problems help with the later ones?" Land: get to the next ten, then add the rest.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this."
Look for: "8 and 2 make a ten." Ask: "How does 8 + 2 help?" Model: numberline 28 +2
Look for: 28 + 2 = 30, then 3 more. Ask: "Where did the 5 go?" Word choice: "I broke 5 into 2 and 3." Model: numberline 28 +2 +3
Look for: 48 + 2 = 50, then 4 more. Ask: "How did you know to use 2?" Model: numberline 48 +2 +4
Look for: 67 + 3 = 70, then 5 more. Ask: "What is the next ten after 67?" Model: numberline 67 +3 +5
Look for: 67 + 3 = 70, then 15 more; or 67 + 10 + 8. Ask: "Can the last problem help?" Model: numberline 67 +3 +15
Look for: the same moves as 67 + 8. Ask: "Predict before I show it. What changed?" Model: numberline 167 +3 +5

strings.title: Split by Place Value
strings.label: Day 2
strings.strategy: Add tens with tens and ones with ones, then put them together. When the ones make more than 10, that makes another ten.
strings.keywords: tens, ones, hundreds, place value, partial sums, make a new ten
strings.connection: Day 1 made a ten on the number line. Today the ones combine into a new ten when we add by place value.
watchFor: Saying "3 + 4" for 30 + 40: ask "Is it 3 + 4 or 30 + 40? How do you know?" and write the real values.
Writing 713 for 70 + 13: ask "How many tens are in 13? Where do they go?"
Forgetting the ones: ask "Did you add every part?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "What happened when the ones added up to more than 10?" Land: 10 ones make a new ten, and it joins the other tens.

problems.notes: Look for: 3 tens + 4 tens = 7 tens. Ask: "How many tens?"
Look for: a known fact, or 6 + 4 + 3. Ask: "How many tens and ones is 13?"
Look for: 70 + 13 = 83. Ask: "How did the last two problems help?" Word choice: "13 ones is 1 ten and 3 ones." Model: text 36 + 47 = 30 + 40 + 6 + 7 ; = 70 + 13 ; = 83
Look for: 70 + 14. Ask: "Where does the extra ten come from?" Model: text 28 + 56 = 20 + 50 + 8 + 6 ; = 70 + 14 ; = 84
Look for: 70 + 13, or 45 + 30 + 8 on the number line. Ask: "Did anyone do it another way?" Model: numberline 45 +30 +8
Look for: 100 + 50 + 12. Ask: "What happens to the hundreds?" Model: text 125 + 37 = 100 + 20 + 30 + 5 + 7 ; = 100 + 50 + 12 ; = 162
Look for: 400 + 70 + 13. Ask: "Which part makes a new ten?" Model: text 356 + 127 = 300 + 100 + 50 + 20 + 6 + 7 ; = 400 + 70 + 13 ; = 483

strings.title: Over the Hundred
strings.label: Day 3
strings.strategy: Get to the next hundred (or ten), then add what is left. Tens can regroup into a new hundred, just like ones regroup into a ten.
strings.keywords: next hundred, friendly number, regroup, 10 tens
strings.connection: Day 1 got to the next ten. Today we get to the next hundred.
watchFor: Writing 1003 for 95 + 8: ask "Is it more or less than 200? Where is it on the line?"
Losing track of the hundreds (186 + 25 = 111): ask "About how big should the answer be?"
Breaking the number awkwardly: accept it, then ask "Which jump would get you to a hundred?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How is getting to the next hundred like getting to the next ten?" Land: 10 tens make a hundred, just like 10 ones make a ten.

problems.notes: Look for: 9 tens + 1 ten = 10 tens. Ask: "How many tens make 100?"
Look for: 95 + 5 = 100, then 3 more. Ask: "Where did you stop?" Model: numberline 95 +5 +3
Look for: the same as 95 + 8, plus 100. Ask: "What is the same? What changed?" Model: numberline 195 +5 +3
Look for: 186 + 14 = 200, then 11 more; or 186 + 20 + 5. Ask: "How did you know to use 14?" Model: numberline 186 +14 +11
Look for: 275 + 25 = 300, then 5 more. Ask: "How many tens did it take to cross 300?" Model: numberline 275 +25 +5
Look for: 275 + 25 = 300, then 13 more. Ask: "Can the last problem help?" Model: numberline 275 +25 +13
Look for: 368 + 32 = 400, then 13; or 368 + 40 + 5. Ask: "Which stops did you choose, and why?" Model: numberline 368 +32 +13

strings.title: Add a Friendly Number, Then Take Back
strings.label: Day 4
strings.strategy: When a number is close to a friendly number (a ten or a hundred), add the friendly number, then take back the extra.
strings.keywords: friendly number, close to, too much, take back
strings.connection: Days 1–3 added up to a friendly number. Today we jump past it and come back.
watchFor: Forgetting to take back (46 + 9 = 56): ask "Is 46 + 9 more or less than 46 + 10?"
Going the wrong way (46 + 9 = 57): ask the same question and show both on the line.
Taking back the wrong amount (135 + 98 = 232): ask "How far is 98 from 100?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "When is this a good strategy?" Land: when one number is close to a ten or a hundred.

problems.notes: Look for: one jump of 10. Ask: "Where did you start and land?" Model: numberline 46 +10
Look for: 46 + 10, then back 1. Ask: "Can 46 + 10 help?" Word choice: "too much by 1, take it back." Model: numberline 46 +10 -1
Look for: 46 + 20, back 1. Ask: "What is the same about 46 + 9 and 46 + 19?" Model: numberline 46 +20 -1
Look for: 46 + 30, back 1. Ask: "Predict how someone will do it." Model: numberline 46 +30 -1
Look for: 135 + 100, back 1. Ask: "Why 100?" Model: numberline 135 +100 -1
Look for: 135 + 100, back 2. Ask: "What changed from the last one?" Model: numberline 135 +100 -2
Look for: 247 + 200, back 2; or 245 + 200 (give and take). Ask: "Which friendly number did you use?" Model: numberline 247 +200 -2

strings.title: Where Does the New Ten Go?
strings.label: Day 5
strings.strategy: Connect mental strategies to the standard algorithm: the carried 1 is a new ten (or hundred) made from 10 ones (or 10 tens).
strings.keywords: regroup, carry, new ten, new hundred, place value, algorithm
strings.connection: Days 1–4 made new tens and hundreds in our heads. Today we see them in the standard algorithm.
watchFor: Writing 512 for 27 + 35 (not regrouping): ask "Is it about 60 or about 500?" and show the 12 ones becoming 1 ten and 2 ones.
Carrying without knowing why: ask "What does that little 1 stand for: one, ten, or hundred?"
Preferring a mental strategy: great. Ask them to show where their new ten is in the algorithm.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "In the algorithm, what is the carried 1 really worth?" Land: it is a new ten (or hundred) made from 10 ones (or 10 tens), the same thing we did on the number line.

problems.notes: Look for: 7 + 3 + 2, or a known fact. Ask: "How many tens and ones is 12?"
Look for: 27 + 3 + 2. Ask: "Where did the new ten come from?" Model: numberline 27 +3 +2
Look for: 50 + 12, or the algorithm. Ask: "In the algorithm, where is the 12?" Model: column 27 + 35 Model: text 7 + 5 = 12 ones = 1 ten and 2 ones
Look for: the same as 27 + 35, plus 100. Ask: "What is the same in the algorithm?" Model: column 127 + 35
Look for: two regroups (ones and tens). Ask: "How many new tens? How many new hundreds?" Model: column 168 + 57 Model: numberline 168 +32 +25
Look for: the same regroups as 168 + 57, plus 100. Ask: "Predict the answer from the last problem." Model: column 268 + 157
Look for: 400 + 226 - 1 (Day 4!), or the algorithm with three regroups. Ask: "Which way was easier here, and why?" Model: numberline 399 +1 +225, and column 399 + 226
